extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers, creative-writing students, and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for revising fiction (especially short stories) to clarify theme and improve craft elements (character, plot, POV, description, dialogue, setting, pacing). Emphasizes multiple drafts, distance before editing, and integrating all choices around the story's theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme: crystallize and integrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Discover and state (or at least crystallize) the theme of the story — e.g., 'True vision is much deeper than the physical ability to see.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make nearly every craft choice (characters, setting, voice, title, opening line, plot progressions, symbol) relate to and reinforce the theme. Show the theme through character actions and plot (theme in motion) rather than stating it. Revise with the explicit aim of making 'all your choices fluidly and delicately flow inside the vessel of your theme.' Symbols should emerge naturally and can be drawn from salient elements (e.g., a cathedral taking on larger meaning). If the chosen theme doesn't visibly connect to the text, consider whether it's too subtle, not illustrated well enough, or simply the wrong theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish a first draft — write with heart, don't edit
rubrics_metrics.description: Get a complete first draft finished; its sole requirement is completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the first draft with instinct and emotion ('with the heart'), be reckless and self-indulgent if necessary, and avoid editing while drafting. Accept that first drafts 'should suck' and reserve critical evaluation for later drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate writing and editing mindsets
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat writing and revising as different disciplines that require different temperaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt distinct approaches (metaphorically different 'hats') for drafting versus revising: the draft-maker should be free and instinctive, the reviser an 'emotionless diagnostician' probing every word with precision. Don't try to edit while you write the first draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the manuscript cool; gain distance before revising
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid revising while emotionally charged or too close to the material; allow time/distance so you can judge the work objectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not revise in the midst of creative ecstasy, anger, exhaustion, or other emotional extremes. Let the manuscript 'grow clammy-cold'—take days or longer, or if time is short use techniques to defamiliarize the text: read aloud to yourself, have someone read to you (preferably a warm body), record and play back, or print in an unusual font. Save all drafts (Woolf's practice) so you can reconstruct earlier versions if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use outside readers/editors judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek sympathetic readers or skilled editors but remember their feedback is ultimately an opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find readers/editors sympathetic to your intentions and style; beware of poor fits or overzealous edits that change your voice. Consider cost and fit; follow good advice but don't obey it slavishly—preserve what is essential to your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision strategy: reenvisioning and multiple drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to rewrite, sometimes extensively; use multiple drafts to discover and refine what you're really writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reenvision the piece—identify its most original or powerful element and consider tossing everything else. Start again from scratch on a fresh document if that helps. You may go through many drafts (dozens in some cases); focus whole drafts on single craft elements (dialogue, theme, etc.) if that is useful. Some stories may need a few drafts, others many—be persistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address the big-picture elements first
rubrics_metrics.description: Before fretting over small copy-editing details, make sure the major structural and thematic elements are right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize 'Big Things'—character, plot, point of view, theme, setting, pacing, and major scenes—before addressing punctuation or line-level choices like dashes or parentheses. Little fixes won't save a story whose big parts are wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: necessary, non-stereotyped, motivated
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure you have the right number of characters, that main characters are fully realized (not flat archetypes), and that they are motivated with clear wants/goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Do I have all the characters I need and no more? Can some be combined or removed? Are characters too flat or fulfilling predictable roles? Are main characters sufficiently motivated (not mere ciphers)? Begin with an individual to avoid creating types. Less is often more—fewer well-developed characters reduce clutter and increase focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot: strong beginning, efficient middle, surprising-inevitable ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Shape plot as beginning–muddle–end; hook readers appropriately at the start, select necessary middle events, and craft endings that feel both surprising and inevitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginnings are crucial—either grab the reader quickly or seduce gently; consider amputating throat-clearing material and begin at the first interesting thing. Middle: select a limited number of telling moments (rule of elegance and efficiency). Endings should be unpredictable yet plausible—reader should react 'My God!' then 'But of course!' Avoid endings that are surprising but impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view: choose the best POV and keep it consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the POV that best serves the material (first person for intimacy/voice, third person for flexibility) and maintain consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask if you've chosen the best POV—should you stick to one character or alternate viewpoints? POV is often dictated by the material, but changing POV can fix a scene that isn't working. Keep POV consistent once chosen and be mindful of each POV's advantages and limits (e.g., who could plausibly tell this story?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: concrete, sensory, selective detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor concrete sensory detail over abstract descriptors; give particulars that evoke sight, sound, smell, taste, and touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abstractions like 'beautiful' or 'mysterious' that put readers to sleep; instead use vivid, specific imagery ('hair streamed like turnings of steaming copper'). Be selective—choose the 'quick' lifeblood details that matter and discard the dead ones. Strong modifiers and inventive compound adjectives can supply concrete jolts of image and sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue: concise, subtext-rich, speakable, and often adversarial
rubrics_metrics.description: Make dialogue economical, full of subtext (what characters mean rather than what they say), natural but not verbatim transcript, and useful for revealing character through conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fewer words to make a point; allow characters' illogical speech when appropriate; favor adversarial exchanges to reveal more. Dialogue must be speakable—read it aloud. Balance dialogue with description and summary; avoid forced lines and let motivated characters 'know what to say and when to say it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting: ground reader in time/place and use metaphorically
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish time and place to orient readers and consider setting as a character or metaphor that supports theme and plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground readers with explicit cues (dates, posters, sensory markers) or subtle signals. Use setting's particularities (e.g., smog for L.A., Spanish moss for New Orleans) to shape tone and influence plot. Employ setting metaphorically to reinforce theme (fog as legal murk in Bleak House, lakes that drown past/present in Housekeeping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene vs summary and pacing: layer and manage for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance scenes (showing) with summary (telling) to control pacing and the reader's experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave scene and summary, knowing the best narratives rise and fall like roller coasters—slow climbs of exposition leading to swift falls of dramatic conflict. Decide which events to compress and which to expand to shape tempo. There is no single right pace; choose what's appropriate for the story's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism: allow symbols to emerge naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Let symbols arise from the story rather than forcing them; a symbol becomes meaningful when it takes on larger significance than its literal presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't worry obsessively about symbols; they often emerge as the writer revises and becomes aware of resonant material. When symbols are present (e.g., the cathedral), use them to amplify theme. The title may signal or crystallize symbolic meaning once it has emerged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know how much to revise—use judgment on revision extent
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise judgment about revision extent: some works need many drafts, others only a few; avoid both excessive fiddling and insufficient revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heed competing maxims: 'Revise till your fingers bleed' versus 'Don't f— with it too much.' Use experience and re-visioning to decide when additional drafts improve the work and when further tinkering risks harm. Some pieces require extensive reworking; others reach their final form sooner.
